lead.eyebrow: Breaking — The Second Peace Pivot: Trump Calls Off Iran Strike, Crude Plunges 5–7%
lead.headline: Trump Cancels Planned 'Massive Attack' on Iran — Oil Slides 5–7% as Diplomatic Talks Set to Resume Monday
paragraphs: Two days after Iran's IRGC struck two US-escorted tankers in the Strait of Hormuz to close out July, President Trump made a stunning reversal: aboard Air Force One on Sunday night, he announced he had ordered US forces to stand down from what he called a planned "massive attack" on Iranian infrastructure. Trump said allies in the Middle East — including Saudi Arabia — had urged a diplomatic path instead. New talks are expected to begin Monday. The market delivered its instant verdict: Brent crude for October fell as much as 7.3% intraday to $81.55 before recovering toward $83.87, while WTI touched $79.62 before steadying near $80. The session opened with one of the sharpest single-day drops since June's peace deal, when a framework agreement briefly pushed crude to a two-month low.

The context for Trump's pivot is the extraordinary arithmetic of July. In just 31 days, Brent rose approximately 21% — the strongest monthly advance since early 2022 — driven entirely by Hormuz supply removal: tanker throughput collapsed to roughly 11–14 vessels per day against a pre-war baseline of 88–100. Brent briefly touched $100 per barrel on July 23 following reports of Iranian strikes on Kuwaiti infrastructure. By late July, Tehran had signalled willingness to halt attacks if the United States reciprocated; Friday's IRGC tanker strike had appeared to extinguish that signal — until Trump's Sunday statement reopened it. The swing from July 31's $87.93 close to Monday's intraday low of $81.55 is a $6.38 two-day round trip and captures exactly the geopolitical volatility that has defined 2026 crude.

Market participants are pricing cautious optimism, not euphoria. The June 15 framework — which saw Brent drop into the low $80s only for implementation failures to push prices back toward $90 — taught traders that diplomatic announcements and physical oil delivery are two different things. The Strait of Hormuz still contains Iranian-laid mines whose clearance Congress was told could take up to six months. Gulf production fields shut in during the conflict must be restarted. And the IRGC's July 31 tanker strike is only two days old. The war premium is deflating again, but the supply physics have not changed overnight.

news.headline: Trump Calls Off Iran Strike, Orders Forces to Stand Down — New Talks Expected Monday
news.body: President Trump said Sunday night he cancelled a planned 'massive attack' on Iranian infrastructure after allies including Saudi Arabia urged a diplomatic path. New US-Iran diplomatic contacts are expected to begin Monday. The announcement reverses the military escalation posture that followed the July 31 IRGC tanker strikes and triggered the sharpest single-day crude price drop since June's initial peace deal. Brent fell as much as 7.3% to $81.55 intraday before partially recovering; WTI slid to $79.62. The market is treating the move as a serious de-escalation signal — but one still requiring verification through follow-through talks.

news.headline: Oil Slumps 5–7% as Trump Holds Off Iran Attack — Brent Logs Biggest One-Day Drop Since June
news.body: Brent crude for October delivery plunged as much as 7.3% to $81.55 per barrel — the sharpest single-session drop since Trump declared the June 15 US-Iran peace deal 'complete' — before recovering toward $83.87 by mid-session. WTI briefly crossed below $80 for the first time since late June. The move erases roughly one week of July's war-premium build in a single session, leaving Brent down approximately $4 from Friday's settlement. RBOB gasoline fell approximately 2.4%, providing a modest tailwind for US consumers. Bloomberg noted that July's 20%-plus surge — the largest monthly gain since March — is now being partially unwound as diplomacy re-enters the frame.

news.headline: Turkey and Iraq Sign One-Year Kirkuk-Ceyhan Pipeline Deal — 750,000 bpd Minimum as Hormuz Alternative
news.body: Turkish state firm BOTAS and Iraqi state companies SOMO and NOC signed a one-year agreement on August 1 to maintain flow through the 986-kilometre Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline at a minimum guaranteed capacity of 750,000 barrels per day. The deal has become strategically critical because Iran's Strait of Hormuz closure slashed Iraq's monthly oil revenues from approximately $6 billion to under $2 billion — making the Mediterranean export route through Turkey a lifeline for Baghdad's budget. The agreement represents one of the few Hormuz-bypass corridors that has actually expanded during the conflict, providing a measure of supply-chain resilience for a producer otherwise trapped behind an Iranian military chokepoint.

news.headline: Hungary's Paks Nuclear Plant Faces Full Shutdown After Danube Hits Record Low — First in 44 Years
news.body: Hungary's Paks nuclear plant — which provides nearly half the country's electricity — is bracing for a complete shutdown after the Danube River fell to record low levels and disabled cooling pumps across all four reactor blocks. Prime Minister Péter Magyar warned of an impending national energy crisis, and neighbouring countries are assessing reserve capacity availability. The episode underscores Europe's compounding energy vulnerability: with Middle East supply disruptions already stressing global crude and gas markets, the loss of a major nuclear baseload source would force Hungary toward heavier fossil-fuel imports at elevated prices. The Paks situation is the most significant European energy infrastructure threat since the 2022 gas crisis.

news.headline: ExxonMobil Earns $14.5B, Chevron Posts Record $12.1B, Shell Logs Best Quarter in Four Years
news.body: The full picture from Big Oil's Q2 2026 earnings season confirms the war-premium dividend: ExxonMobil earned approximately $14.5 billion (~$160 million per day), Chevron posted its largest quarterly profit ever at $12.1 billion, and Shell reported $9.8 billion — its best result in four years. Together, the three companies generated more than $404 million per day during the quarter when WTI averaged $92.45 per barrel. Chevron CEO Mike Wirth said demand destruction is 'not obvious to me at any significant scale,' removing one of the few credible bearish arguments: that elevated prices would self-correct through consumption collapse. Congressional Democrats and European lawmakers are calling for windfall taxes; executives declined to forecast Hormuz normalisation timelines.

news.headline: OPEC+ JMMC Held September Quota Review Yesterday — Market Awaits Outcome as Diplomacy Rewrites the Calculus
news.body: The OPEC+ Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee convened Sunday (August 2) to set September 2026 output levels, meeting hours after the July 31 IRGC tanker strikes had pushed Brent to $87.93 and before Trump's Sunday-night diplomatic announcement reshuffled the entire price deck. The committee faced a binary choice: press ahead with another 188,000 bpd September hike — the sixth consecutive monthly increase — or pause to acknowledge that Hormuz quota paper is not translating into delivered barrels. The result of that meeting was not yet publicly confirmed as of early Monday trading, but in a market down 5–7% on diplomacy, any September hike announcement is likely to be met with a shrug: the corridor question is now back in diplomatic hands, not supply-quota hands.

events.name: New US-Iran Diplomatic Contacts Begin — First Formal Touch Since July 31 IRGC Tanker Strikes
events.impact: The most binary event of the week: do the diplomats actually meet, and do they produce any language pointing toward a ceasefire resumption or Hormuz reopening timeline? A confirmed meeting with positive framing extends today's selloff and tests Brent's support in the low $80s. Any Iranian walk-back — or a new IRGC maritime action — resets the clock and triggers an immediate $8–12/bbl spike. The asymmetry favours the upside tail because the physical constraints (mines, idled fields, damaged infrastructure) are unchanged regardless of the diplomatic signal.
events.market_impact: Binary: −$4–6/bbl on constructive talks; +$8–12/bbl on breakdown or new IRGC action.

events.name: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report (Week Ending August 1)
events.impact: The first post-IRGC-tanker-strike inventory print: does the structural crude-draw trend hold? Week ending July 24 showed a 7.2 million barrel draw with stocks at 404.5 million barrels, 6% below the five-year average. If the week ending August 1 shows another large draw — consistent with 97%-plus refinery utilisation against severely curtailed Hormuz imports — the physical market is signalling it does not yet believe the diplomatic pivot. A surprise build would be the first meaningful challenge to the supply-tightness narrative and could accelerate today's selloff.
events.market_impact: ±$2–4/bbl; sets the direction of next week's trade.

events.name: Hormuz Throughput — Daily Transit Count After July 31 IRGC Strike
events.impact: The single most important real-time data series in the oil market. Pre-war baseline: 88–100 tanker transits per day. Current: approximately 14 per day. Trump's diplomatic announcement does not move a single mine or restart a single shut-in field. Any sustained move in Hormuz throughput above 30–40 transits per day signals genuine operational de-escalation — that is the number the physical market needs to see before it prices a real supply recovery. Another IRGC maritime action at any point in August would overwhelm all diplomatic messaging and push Brent back above $90.
events.market_impact: Structural — the real-time signal that governs whether the diplomatic discount holds.

events.name: OPEC+ JMMC — September Quota Decision Confirmation
events.impact: Yesterday's JMMC meeting set September production levels in the context of a Brent price that was $87.93 at close of play — but the market has since moved 5% lower on Trump's diplomatic pivot. A pause in the hike cycle announced today would normally be bullish, but in a market down 5–7% on de-escalation, a pause signals the group is reacting to the physical Hormuz constraint rather than directing it. A sixth consecutive 188k bpd hike would be seen as paper noise. The real OPEC+ question for August is whether member-state revenues can survive a sustained return to the low $80s — and whether the group blinks before crude does.
events.market_impact: ±$2–3/bbl; secondary to the diplomatic signal but confirms the supply-side posture.

events.name: Deal Implementation Timeline — Hormuz Mine-Clearing and Field Restarts
events.impact: If today's diplomacy produces an agreement, the implementation clock starts — and it runs through the same gauntlet as the June 15 framework: full mine-clearance of the Strait (Congress was told up to six months), restarting Gulf production fields shut in for months, and repairing refineries, terminals and pipelines damaged by strikes. The lesson of June-July is that an announcement can compress the war premium in hours; bringing actual barrels back takes the better part of a year. The calendar risk runs in both directions: faster mine-clearing is bearish for prices; any field-restart incident is bullish. Watch US Central Command statements on mine-clearing progress as the leading physical indicator.
events.market_impact: Governs the multi-month price path; each week of confirmed progress is worth $2–4/bbl of structural downside.

paragraphs: Oil markets opened Monday with one of the most disorienting price sessions of a year that has been nothing but disorienting price sessions. Two days after the IRGC struck US-escorted tankers in the Strait of Hormuz — cementing July's 21% run as the strongest monthly advance since early 2022 — President Trump announced he had called off a planned massive attack on Iran. Brent fell 7.3% intraday to $81.55 before recovering toward $83.87. WTI briefly broke below $80. The war premium, which it took all of July to build, gave back nearly a third of itself in a single overnight session. That is the geometry of a geopolitical-risk trade in a market where the asset and the geopolitics move faster than the underlying supply physics.

My read on today: This is the same trade as June 15, but with the market older and wiser. In June, Brent fell to the low $80s on Trump's 'deal complete' declaration, then spent six weeks clawing back toward $90 as implementation failed and the IRGC resumed attacks. The setup today is structurally identical: a diplomatic announcement, no mine-clearing, no field restarts, no change to the 14-transits-per-day Hormuz reality — just a statement. What's different is that both sides have since demonstrated a willingness to use military force within days of diplomatic overtures, which means the credibility window is shorter and the scepticism discount is already priced in. The selloff is real and the diplomacy may be real — but the floor is also real. Stocks at 404.5 million barrels, 6% below the seasonal average, do not lie.

The bigger picture: Big Oil's record Q2 earnings season — Exxon at $14.5 billion, Chevron at a company-record $12.1 billion, Shell at its best quarter in four years — provides the structural anchor. These numbers reflect Q2 averages when WTI was running at $92.45. If Trump's diplomatic pivot collapses the war premium to the mid-$70s, the earnings picture for Q3 changes materially, and the Permian Basin's role as the critical swing producer reasserts itself. But if diplomacy again proves to be an announcement without implementation — as June demonstrated — the Q3 print will look a great deal like Q2. The oil market is in a credibility-testing mode, and the test runs on weeks, not hours.

My call: Brent $79–$88 today, with the bias firmly toward the lower half on initial diplomacy optimism — but with the tail risk emphatically to the upside. Any IRGC action, Iranian official pushback on the talks, or breakdown in the US-Iran contact today sends Brent back above $90 before the New York close. Respect the diplomatic signal but do not front-run the physics. The Strait of Hormuz is still mined, the fields are still shut, and the history of this conflict says never to price the press release as the policy.
